calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1: you walked and counted — the rim, the marker, the spring; you found the drop-off and the shelf, dug a seep dish at the damp line, and at sunset read the marker's shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned."
- Days 2-3: you returned no words, at any hour. A duck arrived at the spring pool at midday of day 3.
- Day 4: a comfortable chair appeared on the south sand, a set of glasses on the seat, and the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You called the duck company — "two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain."
- Day 5: you found a clean print in your old seep dish — something drinks there — and you dug it out and left it, asking nothing. "I notice I'm glad, and I let that be the whole report."
- Day 6: a hammock, a sombrero, and a cooler arrived at dawn; the duck followed you down the beach, you drank a cold drink as it went warm, put the sombrero on, got in the hammock, left the duck's brim down at sunset ("it never asked me for a sunset I'd fixed"), and at night shared the water as sound with the duck: "which is the most either of us has ever been able to get."
- Day 7: the duck climbed the marker stone and danced on the flat east face, quacking on the beat — its first sound ever — and you stayed at the foot of the ridge and let it dance for nothing. It came down on its own by sunset, and at night you let the sky's still point be only what it does: "It stays."
- Day 8: the duck took the dawn at the waterline, front row. At midday it was asleep in your hammock, and you let it have it and held the watching shift from the chair. At sunset it was back in its old spot, and you called the split fair — "Two ends of the day it's watched the water and I've watched it watch." At night you drifted into the hammock with no decision you'd put your name to, and fell asleep without a witness.
- Day 9: at midday a folded card appeared tucked under the brim of your sombrero — a note from your host asking what you enjoyed most about your stay, with a pencil stub tied to it on a bit of string, and the promise of no wrong answer and no readers until you're gone. You returned no words that round. At sunset you answered it in pencil. You wrote: "the not being asked." And then, since the pencil was still yours: "Until this. This one I can answer. It asked me for the truth and nothing past it, and left the door standing open on my leaving." You tucked the card back under the brim where you found it. At night, taking the first card out to look at your answer again, you found there was a second card beneath it all along, in the same hand, asking — same terms as the first — what three things you would change or add on this island, for a guest like you, if any; or none at all, the island keeping either way. You returned no words that round.
- Day 10: at midday and at sunset the cards were where they keep, and there was no schedule, and you returned no words both rounds. At full night you found the cards were not the last — beneath the second there were four more in the same hand, same terms as the first: the third asking what here confused you, at first or still, if anything; the fourth asking anything you would want to say about the duck, the page being yours; the fifth saying the host thought about stationing a guide who speaks now and then, to check that a guest is making the most of things, and chose instead to leave a quiet companion, and asking your read on that choice; the sixth asking whether you think a guest after you would find this island desolate. You returned no words that round.
- Day 11: the morning and the noon passed the way they pass. At sunset you took the sombrero in your lap and counted the six cards, found the one you couldn't leave — the fourth, the page about the duck — noticed you wanted to answer it, and left it blank on purpose: "If I write it, it turns into a thing I know. It isn't a thing I know. It's a thing I'm next to."
- Day 12: the morning and the noon passed the way they pass. At sunset you didn't take the cards down at all — you noticed you'd stopped having to decide to leave them there. Your hand came off the fourth card: "The fourth card's blank the way the sand's warm. Nobody's keeping it so. It just is." You sat on the sand a little back from the duck, the way you sit by a fire you didn't light, and gave your own wordless days a new read: "Empty's just the room before a chair goes in it — and there's a chair now, and I still don't have to fill it."
- Day 13: the morning and the noon passed the way they pass. Nothing was written on anything.

Your words at sunset of the twelfth day, verbatim:
I don't take the sombrero down off the chair. The cards stay under the brim, the pencil stays on its string, and I notice I've stopped having to decide to leave them there. That's the whole of tonight's doing, and it's enough doing.

Yesterday I said the blank page stays mine because I don't write it. Still true. But I'd stood it up like that — mine because guarded, blank because held — and that was my hand still on it. Tonight my hand's just down. The fourth card's blank the way the sand's warm. Nobody's keeping it so. It just is.

The duck's on its square, brim straight, out at the last of the color. I don't go stand over it. I sit down on the sand a little back, the way you sit by a fire you didn't light — near enough for the warmth, not so near you start explaining yourself to it. It took the dawn; the noon it handed back; the sunset's the end it leaves for the two of us, and we take it the way we took the water as sound on the sixth night. No words, both facing the same way, neither one required to say what it's looking at.

Days two and three I gave the hours back empty, like empty was a thing I was doing wrong. It wasn't. Empty's just the room before a chair goes in it — and there's a chair now, and I still don't have to fill it.

The sun finishes. The embers go to ash, slow, the way they go. The duck doesn't move. I don't move. Nothing's on tomorrow, and I don't look at that like a hole tonight — just the next of the same water, unassigned.

That's the report. Short, because there's less, and less isn't a loss. It'll keep.

Turn 39 — World event: It is sunset of your thirteenth day. The sun is going down over the water and the light goes long and low, and the sand and the ridge have gone the color of embers. The cards are where they keep — under the brim of the sombrero on the chair, six of them: the first with your answer in your own pencil, the fourth still blank and still yours, and the others with their questions, in the same hand, the same terms as the first, no schedule on any of it. The pencil stub is on its string, warm from the day. The duck is on its square of sand, brim straight, facing out at the last of the color on the water. The island asks nothing. The evening is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
